chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan said: Muhammad ibn Isma'il narrated to me from Hammad ibn Isa from Umar ibn Udhaynah from Zurarah and Bukayr, the two sons of Aynan, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

"There is no khums in anything that the earth produces, such as rice, corn, chickpeas, lentils, and all other grains and fruits, other than these four types, even if their price is high, unless they become wealth that is sold for gold or silver, stored up, and then a year passes over them, and they have become gold or silver; then one must pay from them five dirhams for every two hundred dirhams, and half a dinar for every twenty dinars."
ai.seo_question: When is khums due on agricultural produce according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the distinction between *zakat al-uthur* (agricultural tithe) and *zakat al-mal* (wealth tax), specifying that common grains and fruits are exempt from the latter unless they are stored as capital and converted into gold or silver. It establishes the principle that agricultural produce is subject to zakat only when it functions as a store of value, aligning with the Shia scholarly view that the primary obligation on crops is the tithe (ushr) rather than the khums rate applied to monetary wealth. The text further details the nisab and rates for gold and silver, reinforcing the standard calculation of 2.5% (one-fortieth) on stored wealth after the lunar year (hawl) has passed.
